newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian leader pledges aid to flooded Manitoba.
newsitem.headline: Canadian leader pledges aid to flooded Manitoba.

text.p: Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien surveyed the Red River flooding in southern Manitoba on Saturday and pledged financial aid to stricken communities.

Chretien's helicopter visit to the flood-stricken western Canadian province highlighted the enormity of the problems. The river has swamped several small rural communities and threatens to overwhelm its biggest city.

"I'm impressed by the will of the people. Everybody is participating and they're ready for a very serious situation," Chretien said in Winnipeg as the city of 650,000 braced itself for the flooding that was slowly headed its way.
Canada may pay up to 90 percent of the costs arising from the disaster, he said. Costs to stricken Manitoba have yet to be estimated.
In the United States, President Bill Clinton asked Congress for $788 million in disaster aid for flood devastated northern states.
Armies of Winnipeg residents continued to throw sandbags in front of homes on Saturday in a massive volunteer effort to shore up the city.

Manitoba government officials said waters from the Red River had covered almost 600 square miles (1,554 sq km) of rural country in the southern part of the province and some Manitobans have taken to calling the region "the Red Sea."
The flooding, caused by twice to three times the normal snow accumulation and quickly melting snow in the northern plains, could be the worst in 145 years.
The usually tame Red River of the North swelled to 22 times its normal flow this month. Rivers across the Dakotas and Minnesota spilled out over the countryside and inundated thousand of homes.
The flood has moved north through the river valley along the Minnesota-North Dakota border toward Lake Winnipeg, devastating Grand Forks, North Dakota, a city of 50,000.

Water began trickling out of taps in Grand Forks on Saturday as river levels continued to recede. Residents hoped it was a sign they would soon have enough water pressure to take a shower, but officials warned the brown liquid was not safe for drinking.
Amid tension on Saturday, Winnipeg residents monitored local television and radio, which have begun 24-hour flood-related coverage.

"You just have this thud in your stomach as you see this lake coming toward you. You just get sick when you see the pictures and you see people's homes in southern Manitoba that are under water," Winnipeg Mayor Susan Thompson said as fire truck sirens wailed and helicopters hovered above one of the most vulnerable neighborhoods along the river.

City officials said the river was expected to reach dangerously high levels as early as Monday and told the residents of about 500 homes in low-lying areas they may have to evacuate in a moment's notice.
The occupants of 54 homes in areas where the river was lapping against sandbags were forced to leave.
Southwest of Winnipeg, battalions of soldiers and 100 bulldozers and graders raced against the clock to raise a 15-mile (24-km) wall of earth by Sunday to protect the southwest part of the city.
But city officials said the barrier, weakened by wet weather and its hasty construction, may not hold and about 8,000 people in a bedroom community may be forced out of their homes.
A 29-mile (46-km) drainage ditch along the eastern edge of Winnipeg, built after two other destructive floods, was expected to protect most of the city.
